What does a US market entry study include, and is it worth it?

Demand, buyers, competition, regulation, routes to market and a clear recommendation. Worth it when the decision is large and the US market is unfamiliar.

By Taz Abbas, Managing Partner · Published October 29, 2026 · B2B Partnerships

The short answer

A US market entry study tells you whether to enter, where to start, who to sell to, how they buy, who you compete with and what route to market fits. It is worth it when the decision is large, the US market for your category is unfamiliar, or you are choosing between several possible starting points. It is not worth it when it only confirms a decision already made, or when it produces a thick report with no clear recommendation.

Why the US needs its own study

The US is not one market. Buying habits, regulations, competitors and distribution channels vary by state, region and industry, and a strategy that works in one segment can fail in the next. Many international companies enter with a plan built from their home market or from general statistics, and discover after spending heavily that their real starting point was somewhere else. A good study is a way of making those discoveries on paper first.

What a good study covers

  1. Demand and segments. Who buys products like yours, how many of them there are, where they are concentrated and which segments are growing. The goal is not one large market figure but a clear picture of the segments you could realistically win first.
  2. Buyers and how they buy. Who is involved in a purchase, what triggers it, what they compare, how long it takes and where they buy from. This shapes your messaging and your route to market.
  3. Competition and pricing. Who already serves these buyers, at what prices, through which channels, and where they are weak. This shows where you have a real opening and what price range you must fit.
  4. Regulation and compliance. Product certifications, labeling, data and privacy rules, import requirements and any state-level differences that affect cost or timing.
  5. Routes to market. Whether distributors, resellers, agents, direct sales or online channels fit your category, and which partners already reach your buyers.
  6. The recommendation. A clear go or no-go, the starting segment and region, the route to market, the first steps and what they will cost in time and money.

How the research is done

Desk research, using industry reports, public data, competitor websites and trade publications, provides the outline. The most valuable insights usually come from conversations: interviews with potential buyers, distributors, resellers and people who know the category. These reveal how buying really works, what buyers think of existing options and what partners would need to take you on. A study built only from published data tends to miss exactly the details that decide success.

When it is worth it

  • The investment in entering is large relative to the cost of the study.
  • You have no established buyers or partners in the US yet.
  • You are choosing between several segments, regions or routes and need a basis for the choice.
  • Your category is regulated, or US rules differ from those at home.
  • You need a credible plan to present to a board, investors or a parent company.

When it is not

  • You already have US customers asking for more, and the question is how to serve them, not whether to enter.
  • The decision has been made and the study would only confirm it.
  • The budget for the study would leave too little for acting on its findings.

In these cases, a lighter piece of work, such as a set of buyer and partner interviews in one segment, may give you what you need faster.

How long it takes and what affects the scope

The time a study takes depends on how many segments and regions it compares, how many interviews it includes, and how regulated the category is. A focused study of one segment can move quickly. A broad comparison across several segments, regions and routes to market takes longer and costs more. Narrowing the questions at the start, for example by ruling out regions you would never enter, keeps the study focused on decisions you will actually make.

Be wary of studies sold as a fixed template. Every category enters the US differently, and the questions that matter for a medical device have little in common with those for a software platform or a consumer product. The scope should follow your decisions, not the provider's standard report.

What to ask a research provider

  1. How many buyer and partner conversations will the study include, and with whom?
  2. Will it end with a clear recommendation, or with data for us to interpret?
  3. How will you size the segments, and what assumptions will you state?
  4. Do you have relationships with distributors and resellers in our category?
  5. What happens after the study: can you help with the first steps?

Making the study useful

Agree on the decisions the study must inform before it starts, and judge it by whether it helps you make them. Share what you already know, including failed attempts, so the work starts from where you are. And plan to act quickly on the findings. Markets move, and a study that sits on a shelf for a year needs to be redone. The best outcome is a clear first step you can take the following month, with the evidence to justify it.
